title: Interview set-up; name and birth data
description: Dale Anderson introduces the interview with Dolly Hartman at Mission Point, St. Mary's, Idaho, in July 1975. Hartman explains the origin of her name Mae 'Dolly' Hartman, her maiden name McDaniel, her 1924 birth in Sheridan, Wyoming, and briefly muses on being an Aquarian.

title: Montana homestead; drought and wartime move west
description: Hartman retraces her family's 640-acre homestead near Decker, Montana, riding horseback six miles to school, and the drought that pushed them to the Vale irrigation project in eastern Oregon. She recalls graduating from Vale Union High School in 1941 and welding in the wartime shipyards to earn college tuition.

title: University of Idaho; joining the WACs
description: She describes arriving at the University of Idaho in 1943, working at the Hotel Moscow making sandwiches and salads, and joining the WACs when her money ran out, motivated by the GI Bill and an adventurous spirit. She recounts being stationed in Las Vegas and Camp Chaffee, Arkansas, flying in the nose of a B-17 over the Grand Canyon, and earning a meritorious achievement plaque as a personnel clerk at the separation center.

title: Leaving the Army; travel and the Indian visitor
description: Hartman explains why she left the Army rather than staying on, and her brothers' advice against overseas duty. She discusses her preference for purposeful travel over tourism, her Scotch-Irish heritage, and the Indian student the family hosted who invited her and her husband to India, an offer they could not accept.

title: Journey to Moscow; Hotel Moscow and Elsie Nelson
description: Hartman tells of leaving the shipyard in May 1943, riding a Greyhound bus from Portland to Moscow, and being struck by the beauty of the green hills. She describes working for Elsie Nelson at the Hotel Moscow, trapping mice for the chef, and Anderson recalls interviewing Nelson herself.

title: Homesick journey to Jordan Valley; family hardships and winter of 1948
description: Hartman recounts her homesick wartime trip from the shipyards: arriving at Jordan Valley at 3 a.m., walking fifteen miles, sleeping under a juniper tree, and arriving at her mother's school on a borrowed pony. She then describes her poor but principled family of nine children, and the brutal winter of 1948-49 when she and her sister Peggy melted snow and sawed down an old barn for fuel while her bedridden father minded her young son.

title: Parents' story; Hazel and Adassa McDaniel
description: Hartman details her parents' backgrounds: her mother Adassa Lehman, born in Deadwood, widowed by cattleman Henry Zimmerscheid; and her father Hazel Ray McDaniel, called Mac, who homesteaded near Devil's Tower and served in World War I. She tells of their marriage in Coffeyville, Kansas, the confusion over her father's gender on Medicare and bank records, and how her parents met at her grandmother's boarding house.

title: Brothers and sisters
description: Hartman lists her half-brothers and sisters—the Zimmerscheid siblings Ted, June, Kenneth, and Carl, and McDaniel siblings Robert, Betty, Jo, and Peggy—with their locations and occupations, including her artist sister June Moskal and Merrill's Marauders veteran Ted. She notes her unmarried sister Peggy chose independence and faced no family criticism for it.

title: Homer Hartman; courtship in the Forest Service camps
description: Hartman introduces her husband Homer Jackson Hartman and describes meeting him while cooking for fifty college students at a blister rust camp where he was a boss. She recounts their secret courtship in the woods, fooling everyone about their wedding date, her earlier marriage and son Steve, and returning to the University of Idaho on the GI Bill to study dietetics.

title: Hobbies and civic service; 4-H and health planning
description: Hartman describes her hobbies—creative cooking, sourdough, winemaking, riding, reading, and hoped-for writing—and her self-determined 4-H project with an Indian girl on Coeur d'Alene foods and culture. She then explains her service on councils, commissions, and the state health facilities review board in Boise, arguing that responsible citizens must help direct federal funding for health facilities.

title: Disaster relief work; volunteer consulting
description: May (Dolly) Hartman recounts her volunteering as on-site director during the Pomeroy, Washington flood and the awards she received from Governor Evans and the Department of the Army's Civil Defense. She explains that she remains a volunteer disaster consultant for the Inland Empire Division covering northern Idaho and Washington.

title: Landowners' association; opposing Wild and Scenic Rivers classification
description: Hartman describes her association of several hundred landowners defending private rights against Forest Service management under the Wild and Scenic Rivers Act. She criticizes the Forest Service for running the study, setting its criteria and planning to manage the valley, and notes the missing economic impact statement and the environmental statement stalled in the Missoula office.

title: Public input fight; alternative regulations
description: She explains how opponents greatly outnumbered supporters at hearings and how the association built a national base with letters from about twenty states. She argues that flood plain zoning under HUD and state Health Department water-quality rules already address environmentalists' concerns, and points to strong cutthroat trout runs as evidence against pollution claims.

title: Property rights stand; writing plans; food preserving
description: Hartman calls the proposal a public land grab for recreation and pledges to spend her life resisting bureaucracy. She describes her hope of writing a rebuttal piece for Reader's Digest, then discusses her canning, freezing and dehydrator before the interview ends.
